opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because I think for a long time people saw research and products as two separate tracks, almost in tension with each other. And I've actually come to see them as much more complementary than that.

When you put a model like Gemini into people's hands, across all sorts of products, you learn things that you simply can't learn in the lab. You see where the model is brittle, where it's inconsistent, where it gets something brilliantly right and then fails on something a child would find trivial. I sometimes call that "jagged intelligence." Real-world usage maps those jagged edges far faster and more thoroughly than any benchmark we could design internally.

Products also force you to care about things that matter for AGI but are easy to neglect in pure research: reliability, memory, long context, planning over many steps, using tools, and understanding the physical world through vision and audio, not just text. A universal assistant that helps you in your daily life has to be multimodal, persistent, and genuinely helpful over time. Those are exactly the capabilities a general system needs. So the product vision and the AGI vision start to converge.

Then there's the feedback loop. You get signals about what people find useful and where the system lets them down, and that informs what we prioritize in the next generation of models. Approached carefully, with privacy and safety at the center, that loop is incredibly valuable.

That said, I'm always careful that products don't pull us entirely toward the short term. Some of the most important breakthroughs, things like AlphaGo or AlphaFold, came from long-horizon, fundamental research that didn't have an obvious product attached. So the balance I try to strike at Google DeepMind is to let products ground us and stress-test our ideas, while keeping enough space for the scientific exploration that I think is still needed. My view is that we may need one or two more genuine breakthroughs beyond scaling to get all the way to AGI. Products tell you where the gaps are. Research is how you close them.

r001.rationale: The response says product feedback informs priorities for the next generation of models, but does not clearly say that ideas from product development feed into core-model training for the next training run.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually one of the most underappreciated parts of the whole story. There's this view that products are a distraction from the fundamental research, and I used to be more sympathetic to that than I am now. What we've found is that the feedback loop is incredibly valuable, and in a way it's a scientific instrument in its own right.

Think about what a product like Gemini in the hands of hundreds of millions of people actually gives you. You get a distribution of real-world problems that you would never construct in a lab. Benchmarks are useful, but they're a narrow slice, and models learn to do well on them in ways that don't always generalize. When people are using the system for their actual work, their coding, their research, planning their lives, you see the failure modes that matter. The long tail. The cases where the model is confidently wrong, or where it can't hold a plan together over many steps, or where it doesn't know what it doesn't know. Those are exactly the capabilities we need to crack for AGI, and products surface them at scale.

The second thing is that products force you to be honest about robustness and reliability. In research you can show a beautiful result that works seventy percent of the time. In a product, that's not acceptable, and that pressure pushes the research in useful directions. Things like grounding, factuality, calibration, memory, tool use, these all got a lot more attention because they were blocking real use, and they also happen to be core to what an intelligent system needs.

And then there's the agents work, which I think is the clearest example. The whole idea of an assistant that can act on your behalf, that can plan, use tools, and operate in a digital environment, came partly from thinking about what a useful product would look like. But solving it properly requires exactly the kind of long-horizon reasoning and planning that we've been chasing since the AlphaGo days. So the product goal and the research goal end up being the same goal.

I'd add that the compute and the infrastructure argument matters too. Having products at Google's scale means the systems we build have to be efficient, and that's driven a lot of the work on distillation, on smaller models, on serving. That in turn feeds back into how fast we can iterate on the frontier models.

Now, I'd be careful to say it isn't the whole picture. There are things, like the fundamental breakthroughs we'll need in continual learning, or in true reasoning and world models, where you need to give researchers the space to go after ideas that won't show up in a product for years. We try to protect that. But the days when I thought of it as a trade-off, research versus product, are gone. Done right, it's a flywheel, and I think it's one of the reasons Gemini has progressed as quickly as it has.

r001.rationale: The response says product feedback shapes research and helps iterate on frontier models, but it does not describe feeding product ideas into core-model training for the next training run.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a very useful feedback loop between building products and doing the fundamental research. When people use Gemini, they bring problems and ways of asking questions that we might never have thought of in the lab. That helps reveal where the system is genuinely useful, but also where its understanding is brittle—where it loses context, struggles to plan, or gives an answer with more confidence than it should.

Those are product problems, but they’re also research problems. If you want an assistant that can help you with something over a longer period of time, you need better memory, better reasoning, and the ability to check whether it’s actually achieved what you asked. Those capabilities seem very relevant to progress toward AGI.

But I wouldn’t assume that improving a product automatically gets us all the way there. You still need fundamental research, and perhaps new breakthroughs. The exciting thing is having those two processes inform each other: research opens up new possibilities, and putting those possibilities into people’s hands helps us understand what’s still missing.

r001.rationale: The response describes product use informing research and exposing capability gaps, but it does not say those ideas feed into core-model training or the next training run.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a very useful feedback loop. When you put a model into a product, you discover what it can actually do for people, where it’s unreliable, and which capabilities are missing. A benchmark gives you one view of intelligence, but someone trying to accomplish a real task often exposes a different set of limitations.

Take an assistant: you’d like it to understand your goal, remember the relevant context, make a plan, and follow through. That pushes you toward things like better reasoning, multimodal understanding, and the ability to use tools. Those are useful product capabilities, but they’re also important ingredients for more general intelligence.

The challenge is to keep that feedback loop connected to fundamental research. Product feedback can tell us where the problems are; it doesn’t necessarily tell us what scientific breakthrough will solve them. I think you need both—the experience of building systems people use and the space to explore ideas whose payoff might be several years away.

r001.rationale: The response says product use reveals limitations and should inform fundamental research, but it does not describe feeding those ideas into core-model training for the next training run.
